value_detail: 'Beer' limited to not more than 4% alcohol by volume or 3.2% by weight (the lower bound was 63/100 of 1% by volume or 1/2 of 1% by weight until 2009 S.B. 187, then 0.5% by volume). Off-premise beer retailers (grocery and convenience stores) may sell only 'beer'; stronger malt beverages are 'heavy beer', which is liquor.
notes: Ceiling verified for every day 2003-05-05 to 2019-10-31 (metadata/legal_history/utah_code_claims.csv): from 2014 in every Historical Code version of 32B-1-102; 2011-07-01 to 2013-12-31 in 32B-1-102 rebuilt from 2010 S.B. 167 and its amendments; 2003-05-05 to 2011-06-30 in Title 32A's definitions section (32A-1-105, its predecessor in the recodification table) rebuilt from the nine 2003-2009 bills that amended it. value_detail: Question: may an ordinary grocery retailer, under its ordinary off-premise retail authorization, sell sealed wine to the public? No. Grocery and convenience stores sell alcohol as off-premise beer retailers; that authorization (local license, and from 2018 a state license) covers beer, wine is 'liquor', and a person authorized to sell an alcoholic product may sell it only as Title 32B authorizes. Special channels are recorded separately: a state-contract package agency (which may be located in another business) is not covered by this value.
notes: Verified for every day 2003-05-05 to 2026-10-06 (metadata/legal_history/utah_code_claims.csv). From 2014: every Historical Code version of 32B-1-102, 32B-7-201 and 32B-4-402. 2011-07-01 to 2013-12-31: those sections rebuilt from 2010 S.B. 167 and its amendments (reconciled to 2013-05-13, then reconstructed: one word differs from the 2014 code). 2003-05-05 to 2011-06-30, Title 32A: 32A-1-105 (wine is liquor; liquor excludes beer) and 32A-10-101 (local licenses to sell beer for off-premise consumption) rebuilt from the 2003-2009 bills and matched to the Legislature's code pages captured by the Internet Archive in 2008 and 2010; 32A-12-202 (sell only as the title authorizes), which no bill amended after 1990, from those code pages and the session inventory (reconstructed). Predecessors from the recodification table (utah_title32a_crosswalk.csv). Supply provisions verified as corroboration over the same days. Reasoning: data/curated/utah/claim_dependencies.csv; claim_exceptions.csv. Before 2003-05-05: not traced.

value_detail: No retail food store may sell wine before July 1, 2016 (Tenn. Code Ann. 57-3-803(a) as enacted by 2014 Pub. Ch. 554).
notes: Enacted text: section 1 of the act (which adds 57-3-803) took effect on becoming law, signed 2014-03-20. Status before 2014-03-20 not traced from pre-2014 statutes.

value_detail: Conditional authorization (local option). Retail food stores may be licensed to sell sealed wine (not over 18% ABV) for off-premise consumption, only in a county or municipality that passed a local referendum (none before the November 2014 general election; the jurisdiction must already have passed a package-store or liquor-by-the-drink referendum) and has full-time police or sheriff coverage. Retail food store: at least 20% of taxable sales from food and at least 1,200 sq. ft. of retail floor space.
notes: Start date from enacted 57-3-803(a). Status after 2016-07-01 not yet verified against later statutes or current code. Local adoption coverage (which jurisdictions passed referendums, and when) unknown. Recoded 2026-10-07 from conditional_or_special_channel to the policy catalog's authorized_local_option (same meaning, more precise value).

value_detail: Retailers licensed under 57-3-204 (package/liquor stores) may sell beer and other malt beverages, and alcohol-related merchandise, beginning July 1, 2014.
notes: Concurrent change in the same act as food-store wine. Prior status (package stores could not sell beer) is implied by 'Notwithstanding subsection (a)' but is not coded.

value_detail: Unfair Wine Sales Law: a Class C misdemeanor for any wine retailer (food store wine licensee or package store) to advertise, offer or sell wine below cost to the retailer, defined as the basic cost of wine plus 20%.
notes: Takes effect the same day food-store wine licenses begin (section 30 of the act). A concurrent price rule that also binds package stores; any analysis of the 2016 change must account for it.

value_detail: Special channel: the commission may direct the department to contract with a private person to sell liquor (including wine) in sealed containers from premises not owned or leased by the state, at state-fixed prices, with the number of agencies capped by population; the type of business in which an agency may be located is a factor in issuing it. Whether any agency is located in a grocery store is an empirical question this value does not answer.
notes: Verified 2003-05-05 to 2026-10-06 (claim ut_package_agency_channel_available): 32B-2-601 and 32B-2-603 from 2011-07-01 (Historical Code from 2014; before that the text of 2010 S.B. 167 as amended by 2011 ch. 307, which matches the 2014 versions); before that their Title 32A predecessors 32A-3-101 (rebuilt from 2003 and 2008 bills, matching the 2008 and 2010 code pages) and 32A-3-104 (no amendment after 1993; text from the 2008 and 2010 code pages, reconstructed). Package agency types are set by administrative rule (R81), not yet collected. Before 2003-05-05 not traced.

value_detail: The department is the only wholesaler of spirits: spirits is liquor, liquor enters the state only through the department, and manufacturers and industry representatives may sell liquor in the state only to the department.
notes: Verified 2003-05-05 to 2026-10-06 (claim ut_liquor_wholesale_by_department): wine is liquor (32B-1-102), liquor enters the state only through the department (32B-4-401), and manufacturing licensees and local industry representatives may sell liquor in the state only to the department (32B-11-208, 32B-11-608), in every version from 2011-07-01 (Historical Code from 2014; before that 2010 S.B. 167 as amended), and in their Title 32A predecessors (32A-1-105, 32A-12-201, 32A-8-106, 32A-8-505) from 2003-05-05. Boundary: the checks establish that every lawful supply of liquor in Utah runs to the department, so the department is the only wholesaler; that retail licensees then buy only from the department is not separately checked. Beer is not liquor and is wholesaled privately (not coded here). Days before 2003-05-05 are unknown.

value_detail: Retail off-premises wine and beer licenses (Code of Virginia § 4.1-209, subdivision 2, A 2 from 2001) authorize the licensee to sell wine and beer in closed containers for off-premises consumption. The section names no outlet type, so a grocery store's eligibility rests on the absence of a restriction (support basis: general license, no_outlet_restriction).
notes: Verified version by version for every day from 1997-07-01 to 2021-06-30 (metadata/legal_history/state_section_versions.csv and state_claim_checks.csv; tests/test_version_ledger.py). Each version's text is the next amending act's print of it, read from the LIS chapter markup (italic insertions, struck deletions); two emergency acts (2006 ch. 153, 2008 ch. 179) give short versions read from their own text. The chapters are those in § 4.1-209's history notes (an archived 2017 page and the current page); each act's print of the earlier text matches the text after the act before it, apart from catchlines, punctuation and a renumbered cross-reference, and each session's prints combine that session's amendments. Every amending act's own text keeps the license. Inference: the license names no outlet type and nothing in the section excludes grocery stores; Board regulations on eligibility were not read. On 2021-07-01, 2020 chs. 1113 and 1114 moved the license to § 4.1-206.3, which names grocery stores (va_ordinary_grocery_wine_listed). Local option elections on wine and beer sales are a separate dimension. Days before 1997-07-01 are unknown, not projected.

value_detail: Code of Virginia § 4.1-206.3 C 1: retail off-premises wine and beer licenses may be granted to a convenience grocery store, delicatessen, drugstore, gift shop, gourmet oyster house, gourmet shop, grocery store, or marina store.
notes: Created by 2020 Va. Acts chs. 1113 and 1114 (approved 2020-04-10), whose third enactment puts the license reforms into effect on 2021-07-01. Verified version by version for every day from 2021-07-01 (metadata/legal_history/state_section_versions.csv): the versions in force are printed by 2022 ch. 78, 2023 ch. 408 and 2024 ch. 105, by the Virginia Law Library page as captured by the Internet Archive on 2024-08-08, and by the current page read 2026-10-07. The section often exists in two dated versions at once ('Effective until July 1, 2024', 'Effective July 1, 2026'); every printed version in every amending act from 2020 to 2024 names grocery stores. The 2026 chapters (327, 719) are on the new LIS only; the Code's 2026 updates list them without an effective-date note, so 2026-07-01. Local option elections on wine and beer sales are a separate dimension.

value_detail: Grocery store wine permit (Ark. Code § 3-5-1802, added by Act 508 of 2017): a grocery store in a wet territory may purchase and sell wine (not over 21%) for off-premises consumption at a single location. Conditions: no more than 20% of gross sales from alcohol (stores above 20% on 2017-01-01 excepted); must offer small farm winery wine; only in a county where retail sale of alcohol was authorized as of 2017-01-01.
notes: Start date from the enacted text: Act 508 of 2017, section 13(a), makes section 6 (new Subchapter 18, §§ 3-5-1801 to -1803) effective on 2017-10-01; checked against the rendered pages 4 and 7. Status after 2017-10-01 not yet verified: later acts amending the subchapter are not inventoried, and the 2025 ABC rulebook (snapshot base_ar_grocery_wine) is a dated snapshot, not history. What grocery stores could sell before 2017-10-01 (small farm winery wine only, per news reports) is not coded. The county condition freezes local wet status at 2017-01-01; wet and dry status itself is a separate dimension.
